strengths: The core contribution is useful and convincing: Gradient Slingshots manipulates feature visualizations through fine-tuning without architectural modifications. Explicitly shaping trajectories between initialization and target regions provides a substantive extension beyond architectural fooling circuits.

The experiments cover CNNs, vision transformers, several datasets, and multiple visualization procedures. Additional attacks on ten ResNet-50 output neurons and transfer to MACO strengthen the evidence beyond selected examples. ResNet-50 achieves substantial semantic redirection while accuracy decreases from 76.13% to 75.13%.

The CLIP case study illustrates a meaningful auditing vulnerability: undesirable classification behavior persists while the corresponding visualization depicts an unrelated concept. This supports the practical warning against relying exclusively on synthetic feature visualizations.

The method is clearly motivated, and the appendix provides extensive optimization settings, data sources, visualization recipes, and computational requirements, alongside an implementation link. Limitations and potential misuse are discussed explicitly; no unresolved material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Preservation of internal mechanisms is not adequately established. Accuracy and class AUROC can remain stable despite substantial representational changes. Most experiments preserve output-layer activations rather than intermediate representations; the CLIP configuration sets w=1, removing the full-layer preservation term. The penguin AUROC increase from 0.50 to 0.62 and changed natural-image rankings also suggest added selectivity. Held-out representation comparisons and causal interventions would better support the distinction between changing explanations and changing mechanisms.

The claim of arbitrary target-image control exceeds the demonstrated reliability. Several targets produce only textures or compositional resemblance, and out-of-distribution targets perform poorly. For ViT-L/32, Table 21 shows improved textual alignment without improved image similarity at the selected setting: CLIP similarity changes from 0.51 to 0.50 and LPIPS from 0.73 to 0.74. Semantic redirection is better supported than faithful reproduction of arbitrary images.

The theory assumes the desired quadratic gradient field rather than establishing that finite-network fine-tuning realizes it while preserving behavior elsewhere. Its connection to implementation also needs clarification: under the stated Euclidean-ball definition, MNIST initialization with per-coordinate standard deviation 0.01 has typical norm approximately 0.28, exceeding the slingshot radius 0.1 in Table 11. Thus the stated initialization is very unlikely to satisfy the lemma's starting assumption.

The proposed defense is a useful consistency check, but its detection effectiveness is not established. Before/after Jaccard overlap measures retrieval stability, not attack-detection accuracy. There are no calibrated thresholds or false-positive measurements on clean, potentially polysemantic features. The feature-discovery and attribution audit described in Section 5 is also hypothetical rather than evaluated end to end.

The ProxPulse comparison is limited to one feature–target pair and two trade-off settings. Matched tuning budgets and ablations of tunnel sampling, preservation, and gradient versus activation objectives would better isolate the source of improvement. Reported error bars capture visualization randomness, leaving variability across independent attack fine-tuning runs unquantified.

Several reporting inconsistencies should be resolved for reproducibility: Table 3 states 100 CLIP visualization runs, whereas Section C.8 specifies 30; Section 5 reports a 0.1% ImageNet preservation subset, whereas Table 10 gives 0.28%.
